dish: plateau de fruits de mer, choucroute au poisson and the 'Tout Nancy' macaron-bergamote-mirabelle dessert
w: Nancy's Art Nouveau temple, opened in 1911 opposite the station and a Monument Historique — Gruber stained glass, Majorelle furniture, Daum lamps, aproned waiters. A grand seafood brasserie of the École de Nancy where the signature 'Tout Nancy' dessert stacks the city's macaron, bergamot and mirabelle. The definitive Nancy dining room.

Nancy's fine-dining reference beside the Pépinière park — a MICHELIN-starred table (one star, 2025) also honoured by the guide for its welcome and service, where the kitchen turns Lorraine and seasonal produce into a precise, contemporary menu in an intimate townhouse.

dish: seafood-driven modern cuisine near Place Stanislas
w: A MICHELIN-Guide address 300 m from Place Stanislas where chef Hervé Fourrière cooks a personal, classically grounded cuisine with a strong hand on fish and produce, in an elegant contemporary-baroque room. A long-running Nancy gastronomic name.

dish: the authentic macaron des Sœurs and bergamotes de Nancy
w: The keeper of the real Nancy macaron — a crackled, almond-only biscuit whose recipe descends from two Benedictine sisters in 1793 — plus the IGP-protected bergamotes de Nancy, mirabelle specialities and pâtes de fruits. A Living-Heritage (EPV) confectioner near Place Stanislas.

The oldest bergamote house in Nancy, founded in 1840 and facing the station beside the Excelsior — a jewel-box biscuiterie-confiserie (its shop an Amélie-Poulain film location) turning out the translucent bergamotes, macarons and gingerbread that define the city's sweet canon.

dish: seasonal market cuisine (menu changes with the market)
address: 18 Rue de la Source, 54000 Nancy, France
w: A young, well-travelled chef runs this laid-back bistro on a cobbled lane near the Basilique Saint-Epvre, with a short blackboard menu that shifts with the seasons and the market — generous, produce-first plates. A MICHELIN-Guide bistro pick in the old town.

dish: quiche lorraine and the Stanislas parfait (macaron & mirabelle)
w: A café-brasserie institution on Place Stanislas since the 1850s, named for a Napoleonic general and reopened in 2024 with its mirrors and velvet intact. Lorraine classics — quiche, mirabelle — and a terrace on the finest square in France; a favourite lunch of critic Gilles Pudlowski.

Strasbourg's historic haute-cuisine address, open since 1840 and once a three-star under Émile Jung — the stuffed crocodile in the window a Napoleonic souvenir. Now a MICHELIN one-star (Relais & Châteaux) where chef Romain Brillat balances classicism and refinement in the city centre.

dish: choucroute garnie, coq au Riesling and baeckeoffe
w: The most famous winstub in Strasbourg, a tavern since 1873 that took Yvonne Haller's name in 1959 — checked cloths, tight tables and the full Alsatian canon: choucroute, coq au Riesling, bibeleskäs, glazed kouglof. A MICHELIN-Guide winstub a step from the cathedral.

dish: choucroute garnie aux cinq garnitures and fried Munster
w: A warm winstub institution on the picturesque Place du Marché-aux-Cochons-de-Lait, plating generous Alsatian cooking — a five-garnish choucroute, spaetzle, vol-au-vent, fried Munster — sometimes with a creative twist. Listed by Gault&Millau.

dish: choucroute and tarte flambée in the tanners' house
w: The most photographed house in Petite France — a galleried 1572 half-timbered tannery that has held a winstub since 1949 — serving the Alsatian repertoire (choucroute, tarte flambée, coq au Riesling) over the canals of the Ill. Setting and plate in one.

dish: choucroute aux trois poissons under Léo Schnug frescoes
address: 16 Place de la Cathédrale, 67000 Strasbourg, France
w: 'The most beautiful house in Strasbourg', a Gothic-and-Renaissance timber landmark of 1427-1589 at the cathedral's foot, listed since 1929 and painted inside by Léo Schnug. A destination brasserie for Alsatian cooking, above all its choucroute of three fishes.

address: 6 Rue du Tonnelet Rouge, 67000 Strasbourg, France
w: The address that gave the tarte flambée its cult revival — thin, wood-fired flammekueche from surrounding farms' produce in a no-frills, buzzy room, opened by Régis Nombret in 2010 (now with a second Binchstub on Place Broglie). A local favourite for the real thing.

A pâtisserie-chocolaterie and salon de thé in the centre, prized for its kougelhopf (sweet and the bacon-walnut savoury version), Alsatian tarts and chocolates. A reliable stop for the region's baking canon; recommended by Gault&Millau and the Alsace tourist board.

dish: Alsace Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Crémant tasting in a 14th-century cellar
n: Cave Historique des Hospices de Strasbourg
w: A 1,200 m² medieval wine cellar under the city hospital, built 1393-1395 and still ageing Alsace wine — home to a 1472 vintage, one of the oldest wines in the world. Taste and buy Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Crémant d'Alsace amid monumental old casks.

address: 6 Rue de la Gare, 67210 Obernai, France
w: The corridor's gastronomic summit — a two-MICHELIN-star table in Obernai where local terroir (foie gras, game, Alsace produce) is elegantly reinvented in a jewel-box dining room. Worth the short trip off the wine road from Strasbourg.

dish: choucroute and braised pork cheeks in beer, in a 1605 house
w: A genuinely Alsatian winstub behind one of Alsace's finest carved-timber Renaissance facades, built in 1605 by the bishopric's receiver Henri Katz. Warm wood, painted decor and the full canon — choucroute, pork cheeks braised in beer, chicken pot pie. A landmark stop at Saverne on the Nancy-Strasbourg corridor.
